Q: Why people use "src" variables in make instead of just an "obj"? A:

You often want to list the source files for operations like updating dependencies as well as building the object files. Since the source files are what you keep in version control, it seems sensible to start with the source file names (hence a src macro) and derive the object file names from the source file names. You may also be dealing with multiple source languages (with different extensions and different compilers), but object files all have the same extension. So, you might have:

FILES.c   = file1.c file2.c
FILES.cxx = file3.cxx file4.cxx
FILES.o   = ${FILES.c:.c=.o} ${FILES.cxx:.cxx=.o}

Q: Notifying programmer to use another function: Alternatives to @Deprecated? A:

... but this always has the feeling of "this method will be useless/gone in 15 years".

That "feeling" is incorrect.

While Sun / Oracle / OpenJDK typically have a long lead time on removal of @Deprecated features, other software providers remove deprecated features on a much shorter timescale; e.g. at the next major release.

As a software provider, you are free to set your own policy for deprecation. Include it in your product's documentation. For example, in the release notes list the classes, methods, etc that are slated for removal, and list the release where they are due to be removed.

Are there any other ways to hint the programmer to use the new function?

The @Deprecation annotation is the way that is most likely to be noticed by the programmer. If they ignore it ... that's on them.

Inventing a novel annotation is likely to have the opposite effect to what you want:

  • Most programmers won't notice the annotation, or understand what it means.
  • Standard tooling (e.g. IDE compilers, style checkers, etc) won't know to treat the annotation specially.

Q: how does aws lambda invoke work A:

AWS Lambda will run your function when you call the Invoke Lambda API action. This call is implemented as a POST request to the AWS Lambda service API endpoint. The call specifies which function to run, the IAM credentials (and signature) to authorise the invocation, and a JSON payload to pass as input to the function.

Your function (or a runtime client that wraps your function) will perform a POST request to the AWS Lambda runtime API next invocation endpoint, and sleep waiting for the response. This response will arrive (allowing your function to wake and continue running) after the next Invoke call and will contain the JSON payload. Your function (or the runtime client that wraps your function) will then post any computed result to the response endpoint, and again attempt an execution-blocking call to the next invocation endpoint.

Various AWS services (including Application Load Balancers, Cloudfront and API Gateway) are each able to proxy HTTP(S) requests to Invoke calls. These services will encode the incoming request parameters into a JSON structure and send it, via the Lambda API service, to your function's runtime. (Note that your function does not attempt to directly listen for HTTP/S requests. The runtime client will parse the JSON payload and from it pass specific fields as arguments to your function.)

Q: How Do You Retrieve a Video Output's Preferred Resolution? (BIOS Bootloader) A:

Use VBE’s EDID call:

• In real-mode/int10h set AX=4F15h, BH=00h, ES:DI→128-byte buffer

• BIOS returns the EDID block; parse the detailed timing descriptor at offset 54 for the preferred (native) resolution.
